tts_text: stick. stick on. stick to. stick with. stick around. stick out. stick up for.
classification_reason: A very common everyday American-English noun and irregular verb; the card emphasizes the learner-requested high-value forms stick on, stick to, stick with, stick around, stick out, stick up for, and be or get stuck.

senses.definition: A thin piece of wood, especially one that has fallen or been cut from a tree.
senses.example: She picked up a stick and threw it for the dog.

synonyms.note: a small, thin branch
usually larger and still attached to or cut from a tree

senses.definition: To attach something to a surface, or to become attached.
senses.example: Stick the grocery list on the fridge.
senses.usage_note: Common patterns: stick A on B and stick A to B. On often emphasizes placement on a surface; to often emphasizes attachment. Irregular forms: stick–stuck–stuck.

synonyms.note: broader and more neutral
more formal

antonyms.note: take something away from a surface

senses.definition: Informal: to put something somewhere quickly or casually.
senses.example: Just stick the leftovers in the fridge.

synonyms.note: neutral and more broadly applicable
more deliberate and slightly more formal

senses.definition: To be unable to move, leave, or make progress.
senses.example: We got stuck in traffic for an hour.
senses.usage_note: It also applies to tasks and problems: I'm stuck on the last question.

synonyms.note: especially when someone is unable to leave
describes being stuck on a task or problem

antonyms.note: continue advancing on a task or problem

senses.definition: STICK TO — to continue following a plan, rule, schedule, diet, subject, or similar established course.

synonyms.note: more formal
natural with plans, rules, and instructions

antonyms.note: move away from an established plan or subject

senses.definition: STICK WITH — to continue using, doing, choosing, or supporting something or someone.
senses.example: I'll stick with my current laptop for another year.

synonyms.note: neutral and broadly applicable
emphasizes continuing despite difficulty

senses.definition: STICK AROUND — to remain somewhere or continue to be present.
senses.example: Stick around after the meeting if you have any questions.

synonyms.note: more neutral
more formal

senses.definition: STICK OUT — to extend beyond a surface or be especially noticeable.
senses.example: That spelling mistake really sticks out.

synonyms.note: natural when something is especially noticeable
used for extending beyond a surface and is more formal

senses.definition: STICK UP FOR — to defend someone or something against criticism or unfair treatment.
senses.example: She always sticks up for her teammates.

synonyms.note: equally common
more neutral

observed_forms: fold the lower-left corner up diagonally
tts_text: fold. fold up. fold over. fold in.
classification_reason: A common everyday noun and verb for clothes, paper, and physical instructions; the card emphasizes the learner-requested constructions fold up, fold over, and fold in.

senses.definition: A line or bent part created when one part of something is placed over another.
senses.example: There was a deep fold in the fabric.

synonyms.note: emphasizes the visible line
does not necessarily create a sharp line

senses.definition: To bend something so that one part lies over another.
senses.example: Fold the paper in half before cutting it.
senses.usage_note: Common combinations include fold clothes, fold a sheet of paper, fold something in half, and fold your arms.

synonyms.note: broader and does not require one part to lie over another
emphasizes creating a visible fold line

antonyms.note: open something that has been folded
make something level and remove its folded shape

senses.definition: FOLD UP — to make something smaller by folding it or to move one part upward by folding.
senses.example: Fold the lower-left corner up diagonally.
senses.usage_note: Separable: fold up the map, fold the map up, and fold it up; not fold up it.

synonyms.note: applies to furniture or structures designed to fold
make something take up less space

antonyms.note: return something to its open position

senses.definition: FOLD OVER — to bend or turn one part so that it lies over another part.
senses.example: Fold the top edge over by two inches.
senses.usage_note: Separable: fold the edge over and fold it over; not fold over it.

synonyms.note: works in some physical instructions
may not result in one part lying flat against another

antonyms.note: return something to its open position

senses.definition: FOLD IN — in cooking, to gently combine an ingredient with a mixture without removing too much air.
senses.example: Gently fold the egg whites into the batter.

synonyms.note: broader and does not describe the gentle folding technique
formal and does not specify how the ingredients are combined
